title: Spatial Transcriptomics on a Diverse Pancreatic Cancer Cohort Reveals Race-Related Differences in Tumor Subtypes and Immune Microenvironments.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a lethal malignancy 20% more likely to develop in Black African Americans (BAA) compared to Non-African Americans (NAA). Large-scale gene expression analysis of tumor subtypes and cellular microenvironments in a diverse PDAC cohort could help provide insights into cell and molecular differences in BAA cancer cells. Here, we conducted a multi-omics interrogation of BAA versus NAA PDAC using whole exome sequencing, spatial transcriptomics (ST), and spatial proteomics. Whole exome sequencing confirmed patient ancestry and showed no significant differences in driver mutations between race groups. BAA PDAC tumors had significantly fewer classical molecular subtype cells with no change in more aggressive basal-like cells. Instead, BAA patients showed a significant enrichment of the intermediate/hybrid subtype compared to NAA patients. BAA tumors also displayed increased B cell and reduced myeloid cell interactions compared to NAA tumors. Analysis of tertiary lymphoid structures in a validation cohort revealed that tumors in BAA patients displayed larger TLS size and number compared to NAA. In conclusion, these findings identify an increased intermediate molecular subtype signature in BAA tumors at the expense of cells with a classical subtype, accompanied by a distinct immune cell composition and spatial distribution. This study highlights that health disparities in patients of different ancestries may have a molecular basis that influences tumor aggressiveness and the immune response, which may inform therapeutic strategies.

title: Spatial Biology and Organoid Technologies Reveal a Potential Therapy-Resistant Cancer Stem Cell Population in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies with a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%. Chemotherapy is the current standard-of-care (SOC) for advanced PDAC; however, treatment resistance driven by a complex and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) limits its effectiveness. Cabozantinib (cabo), a multi-kinase inhibitor has shown promise in preclinical PDAC models and clinical trials, particularly when combined with immunotherapy, but its mechanisms of action within the PDAC TME remain unclear. Using CosMx Spatial Molecular Imaging and Orion Multiplex Immunofluorescence, we analyzed PDAC tissues collected from patients after first line systemic chemotherapy and surgery, or liver metastatic sites. Matched patient-derived organoid (PDO) co-cultures harboring cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and autologous immune cells (IMM) (PDO/CAF/IMM) were generated and used to evaluate the effects of cabo and anti-PD1 immune checkpoint inhibitor pembrolizumab. Spatial analyses of post-chemotherapy and metastatic PDAC tissues revealed heterogeneous cell neighbor-hoods within the TME, including enrichment of Schwann cells, CAFs, T regulatory cells, and cancer stem cells (CSCs). Distinct niches were observed in metastatic liver tissues, characterized by CSCs expressing CD44 and TROP2. In PDO/CAF/IMM co-cultures, treatment with cabo in combination with pembrolizumab enhanced cancer cell death by depleting myeloid-derived suppressor cells and promoting cytotoxic T lymphocyte proliferation. Both patient tissues and treated co-cultures showed a persis-tent SOC-resistant CSC population that expressed CD44 variant 9 (CD44v9). This in-tegrative spatial and organoid-based approach demonstrates that cabo potentially re-models the PDAC TME to potentiate PD-1 immunotherapy, while revealing therapy-resistant CD44v9+ CSCs as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Survival-associated cellular communication networks in human solid cancers
abstract: Single-cell atlases have enabled the prediction of human cell-cell communication (CCC) networks in cancer, but whether predicted communication networks have clinical significance is not well understood. Here, we integrated a pan-solid cancer scRNA-seq atlas comprising 78 cell types from 318,426 quality-controlled cells with bulk RNA-seq and clinical outcome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to develop Single-cell-based Kaplan-Meier Analysis Network (SKyNet). SKyNet prioritizes ligand-receptor interactions associated with overall survival across 11 human solid cancers, predicting unique interactions not inferred by previous CCC algorithms. In pancreatic adenocarcinoma, SKyNet-predicted endothelial-pericyte interactions were associated with poor outcomes that were validated by independent spatial transcriptomics and survival cohorts. In lung adenocarcinoma, lymphatic endothelial cell interactions consisting of collagen-integrin pairs were associated with poorer survival outcomes. In kidney renal clear cell carcinoma and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma, fibroblast communication networks displayed disparate survival associations, with the DSC2-DSG2 axis associated with better survival outcomes. Thus, SKyNet provides a hypothesis-generating framework for cell type-specific communication pathways associated with patient outcomes.
